study_notes.topic: Quantity Comparison (Q1 vs Q2) - Quantitative Aptitude

sections.title: Intermediate Concept: Arithmetic Word Problems
sections.content: At Level 2, Q1 and Q2 are framed as standard arithmetic word problems (Time & Work, Profit & Loss, Simple/Compound Interest, Mixtures). You must apply arithmetic concepts rapidly to extract the comparative values.

sections.title: Base Equalization in Percentages
sections.content: When comparing percentages or fractions, ensure the 'base' (total value) is the same. If Q1 is a profit percentage on a Cost Price of 500, and Q2 is a profit percentage on a Cost Price of 800, you must calculate the absolute profit value if the question asks for 'Profit Amount'.

sections.title: Ratio Method for Comparison
sections.content: If both quantities are based on the same underlying variables, use ratios instead of absolute values. For example, if Q1 is the speed of Train A and Q2 is the speed of Train B, and you know their time ratio is 3:4 for the same distance, their speed ratio is 4:3. Hence Q1 > Q2 without finding exact km/hr.

sections.title: Time, Speed & Distance (TSD) Logic
sections.content: In TSD, use logical proportionality. If Distance is constant, Time and Speed are inversely proportional. Use this logic to compare quantities without writing out full equations.

sections.title: Time and Work 'LCM' Strategy
sections.content: For Time & Work comparisons, assume the Total Work to be the LCM of the given days in both Q1 and Q2 simultaneously, even if they are separate scenarios. This standardizes the 'units of work' and makes comparing efficiencies much faster.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Solving a Profit & Loss problem for the exact Selling Price when only the Profit Percentage was required for comparison. 2. Ignoring the units (comparing minutes in Q1 to hours in Q2). 3. Getting bogged down in heavy arithmetic instead of using ratio logic.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 2 integrates word problems into the Q1/Q2 format. The key is establishing relationships (ratios, percentages) rather than finding absolute standalone numbers. Always verify that the units of measurement in Q1 and Q2 match before comparing.

short_tricks.topic: Quantity Comparison (Q1 vs Q2) - Quantitative Aptitude

tricks.title: The Percentage Base Trick
tricks.explanation: If comparing two percentage values of different bases, use the 1% rule or fraction values quickly. Do not do full multiplication.
tricks.example: Q1: 44% of 550. Q2: 56% of 450. Think: Q1 is approx 50% of 500 (250). Q2 is approx 50% of 450 (225). Q1 > Q2.

tricks.title: Cross-Multiplication for Fractions
tricks.explanation: When Q1 and Q2 result in fractions, do not convert them to decimals. Cross-multiply to compare them instantly.

tricks.title: Unit Check Elimination
tricks.explanation: Before doing any math, look at the final unit requested. If Q1 asks for Time and Q2 asks for Speed, they are asking for a numerical magnitude comparison. Be careful not to assume physical relationship constraints.
tricks.example: Q1 = 40 km/hr. Q2 = 45 hours. Numerically, 40 < 45. Q1 < Q2.

tricks.title: The 'Constant Difference' Logic in Ages
tricks.explanation: In Age problems, the difference between the ages of two people is always constant. Use this rule to bypass equations.
tricks.example: Q1: A's age when B is 30. Q2: B's age when A is 30. If you find A is older than B initially, Q1 will ALWAYS be > Q2.
